newsitem.title: GABON: Slow start to Gabon parliamentary poll.
newsitem.headline: Slow start to Gabon parliamentary poll.

text.p: Voting began slowly in Gabon's much-delayed parliamentary elections on Sunday with polling stations experiencing problems over voting materials and none opening on time, officials said.

Witnesses reported a low early turnout and a heavy deployment of security forces in the capital Libreville, where the main opposition National Woodcutter's Rally won chaotic local elections in October.
The elections are part of a timetable of democratic and electoral reforms brokered in Paris after violence marred President Omar Bongo's 1993 re-election.

"It's simply a question of time," an electoral official told Reuters in the capital of the oil-producing Central African nation, an hour after the notional 7 a.m. (0600 GMT) start time. Libreville polling stations began opening shortly afterwards.
More than 1,000 candidates were bidding for 120 seats in the national assembly. Gabon, a former French colony of 1.2 million people, has an electorate of about 500,000.

Opposition parties, while playing a full part in the elections, have denounced delays in issuing voter cards and displaying electoral lists. Under the electoral law, this must be completed eight days before polling.

Sunday's vote will be Gabon's second multiparty legislative polls. The first were in 1990 when a wave of democratic reform swept across Africa after the fall of communism in the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe.
Bongo has ruled the former French colony since 1968 after the death of Gabon's founding head of state, Leon Mba.
Witnesses said security forces were out in far greater numbers in the capital than during the October elections.
The head of the electoral commission, Antoine Nguema Essone, told state television late on Saturday the deployment was to ensure disciplined and peaceful polling.

Electoral commission officials said in Akieni in the south, Bongo's stronghold, voting material had been vandalised and was being replaced by plane as were missing ballot papers for a candidate in Minvoul in the north.
Bongo's Democratic Party is expected to face strong competition from the Woodcutters Rally, led by Father Paul Mba Abessole, a Roman Catholic priest and runner-up in 1993.
That election triggered opposition protests in which at least five people died.
Pay protests turned violent and political in early 1994. The official death toll was nine, the opposition put the toll at 38.
Sunday's polls were due to close at 7 p.m. (1800 GMT). Based on past experience, results could take a week to trickle out.
